en: A star moved in the sky.
To Manas, gone to the hereafter,
He had been a friend for eternity.
They pursued their claims together,
Waged war upon their foes together,
Went scouting together,
Took horses from foreign speakers.
They united when tiny as lice,
Joined when little as thumbs.
They stepped over the edge of a sword.
To Manas, gone to Judgment,
He swore oaths forty times over.
He settled Talas and made it a town,
Destroyed the enemies who opposed him,
Made tamarisk-covered Keng-Kol his land.
Meeting him at nine years old,
He made mighty leopard Manas a hero.
He summered in middle Keng-Kol,
Tethered plunging winged steeds.
Misfortune boiled for those who met him.
Those who roused his anger
He drove before him.
Those who committed great wrongs
He put between his fangs and chewed.
The elder of the Muslims,
Khan Koshoi of the Katagan,
He honored as an elder.
On hearing news of him,
The khan of lower Kanggai wept.
Meeting face to face, they became friends.
When his valor became known,
The khan of Beijing stirred.
He drove white deer and made them cattle.
When his precious Manas was alive,
He threw fighting enemies into turmoil.
He drove gray deer and made them cattle.
When his fierce wolf was alive,
He threw his chosen target into turmoil.
A lion supported by his holy patron,
Against all the world
He was a hero whose strength sufficed.
His wings were broken back;
This was his time of ruin,
Parted from his Manas.
From places he besieged he took gold coins;
He took elephants laden with gold coins.
When his blood-shedding hero was alive,
He took a thousand dark-eyed captives.
He poured blood into clear water,
Set grassy places ablaze.
He broke Omsk and took booty.
When his destroyer was alive,
He broke through the middle and made a road.
Hardened by drinking blood,
He was called the leopard Bakai.
Told to take a cap, he cut off a head;
Told to spill stomach contents, he spilled blood.
When he reached eleven,
He broke royal courts and took booty.
When he reached twelve,
He became khan of a people with a royal court.
Holiness came to dwell in Bakai;
He became a soul of saintly birth.
Parted from his destroyer,
Bakai was then abased.
His wings were broken back;
He was parted from his blood-shedding Manas.
He was parted from his twin;
It was the time God took his twin.
He had no garden planted in Talas;
Almambet and Chubak were gone as well.
He had no strength to gird himself;
His renowned lion Manas was gone.
It was the time God took the warrior,
The time your Bakai was left alone upon the ridge.
'My warrior entrusted this to me,' he said.
It was the time your Bakai tended camels.
At Zhangyryk's Zhar-Kyya,
On the trail wide enough for a single horse,
At Besh-Tash's head, a fine summer pasture,
High upon the mountain ridge,
The valiant, fierce-wolf Bakai
Had five hundred households under his hand.
'My fierce wolf Manas has died,' he said,
Weeping greatly wherever he went.
His eyes had grown inflamed with pus;
His chest had grown rattling.
Blessed holy Bakai—
It was the time he laid his head on a pillow,
The time he lay grieving.
Where people gathered he did not approach;
It was the time Bakai withdrew into himself.
It was the time Bakai shunned assemblies.
Where meetings formed he did not approach.
Your fierce-wolf Bakai, withdrawn,
It was the time he fled into seclusion.
The Argyn and Kyrgyz, his ancestral people—
Bakai never came before them.
'They are my people left by the generous one,' he said,
But he never came to the six villains.
Your lion Bakai, the leopard,
Never looked upon the six villains' faces.
Abyke, Köbösh—the six villains—
If they imposed tribute and used force,
He would not pour them a cup of tea,
Would not give a mangy yearling from his horses.
Let alone tribute, he would not give a stone;
He would not bow his head to the six villains.
His own Argyn and Kyrgyz people,
He would not let winged creatures strike,
Would not let beaked creatures peck.
He would not let them graze broken-headed grass;
He would not let them feel the lack of Manas.
A star separated from the sky;
Light poured onto the earth.
Stars came singly from the sky,
Trembling toward the direction of prayer.
Stars cried out from the sky,
Quivering toward the direction of prayer.
Dawn broke and swelled;
Behind the dawn the light bulged forth.
Dawn split open bright and clear;
Light poured onto the earth.
Starting awake from sleep,
Then the leopard Bakai
Turned upon his right side,
Rose and performed his prayers,
Saddled his gray winged steed,
For the only child gained after mortal struggle,
For Semetey, he felt alarm.
His heart pounded without pause:
'If my death has come, let me die.
My orphan and my widow—
Let me see my Semetey.
Let me set their affairs in order.
My orphan left by the hero,
Let me ask after my Semetey.
Without once seeing Semetey's eyes,
How could I remain alive?
Let me saddle my winged steed properly.
My falcon child Kanykei—
Without delay, let me recite the Quran.
My sworn mother Chyiyrdy—
Let me return and offer counsel.
The beauty among the dark-complexioned,
The lovely one among the Muslims,
My dear child Kanykei—
Let me meet her once and return.
Let me see my widow;
Let me kiss my orphan.
My banner fastened to a spear,
My gift left by generous Manas,
Let me see my orphan;
Let me offer him help.
Taking the only child to my breast,
Let me go and cherish him once.'
The winged steed beneath him
He whipped every which way,
Spurring it from either side,
Breaking up the face of the earth,
Galloping on the gray winged steed.
When it reached a downward slope,
Khan Bakai's gray winged steed
Planted its forelegs like a roe deer.
As it pressed uphill,
Its mane and tail spread out,
Its hoofs thundered on the earth.
The black steel bit
Clattered in its throat.
Its mouth gaped like a ravenous maw;
White foam mixed with blood
Splashed upon its breast.
The ground it trod broke apart.
Its flying clods, like little cauldrons,
Whirred overhead.
The banner floated in his hand;
The black steel all-cleaving sword
Flashed across his back.
Dear leopard Bakai,
To Kainar's dark spring-eye,
To the very plane tree,
Below Tört-Kül,
To the garden Lord Manas planted,
To the throne the hero occupied,
Came galloping up.
When he arrived at a gallop,
All its willows had been felled,
All its buildings pulled down;
They had utterly plundered it.
Leveling the royal court flat,
They had plundered it long before.
Breaking the stone city,
They had utterly sacked it.
Jutting up here and there,
Only traces of the palace remained.
Kanykei's white palace,
Its gate of iron and solid tin—
Tört-Kül had become a mound.
Someone had come long before
And killed the orphan.
They had taken all the plunder;
They had wreaked such destruction.
Not a crow gave a caw;
Not a raven gave a croak.
Only an empty plain remained.
'God, stop digging my pit;
God, do not boil my misfortune.
In a plain where no owl flies,
Was this the day to know loneliness?
Parted from my only Semetey,
Was this the day to stand forlorn?
From a plain where no dust flies,
Returning without delay,
God, why have you left me desolate,
Parting me from my only Semetey?
If I travel for nine months,
My Buraq to saddle and ride,
When holy men assembled,
My lamp brought into being by their blessing!
If I travel for six months,
My Buraq to ride afar,
From his elder, the hero Koshoi,
My lamp obtained by asking!
O my banner, my valiant one,
My only one left by the generous hero!
Set before me, my fortunate road;
Walking behind me, my countless army!
O Semetey, my flower calf,
My dark-browed young falcon,
'To equal Manas,' I said,
My lamp whom I held close!
My cherished flower calf,
I made my words a pledge:
'The only one the warrior left,' I said,
And made you my support.
Has the support at my waist broken?
In my destitute old age,
Has God struck me down?
My beard that enemies dared not approach—
Have magpies and ravens shorn it?
Has my lighted candle gone out?
My only child Kanykei—
Have enemies carried her away as booty?
In Chyiyrdy's old age,
Have they cut her up for the dogs?
My widow and my orphan—
Having failed to come and see them earlier,
This Bakai standing here—
Have enemies shorn his beard?
My wings broken back,
How shall I remain alive,
Parted from my queen Kanykei?
When they took their fill of wealth,
Acquiring much gold, I was not there.
Destroying the orphan's possessions,
When they raided, I was not there.
